Bustamante's attorney, Mike Torres, said a warrant was issued for Bustamante's arrest after he failed to appear at a court hearing last week. "He was a familiar face around the federal courthouse here," Torres said. "I'm very shocked by this and very saddened. "He had a lot of friends and a lot of people that cared about him." Carter said Bustamante was on "modified status" with the marshals, meaning he had been required to turn in his gun and badge outside of his official work hours. "What I can tell you is that the U.S. Marshals Service is saddened by the death of Deputy Bustamante and our thoughts and prayers are with his family," he said. According to Carter, Bustamante had been placed on administrative leave and ordered to surrender his firearm and badge—a condition Carter termed "modified status," applicable during non-working hours. Carter clarified that Bustamante's presence in Mexico wasn't connected to official marshal duties, and confirmed investigators had already recovered all the stolen weapons named in the charges.

"What I can tell you is that the U.S. Marshals Service is saddened by the death of Deputy Bustamante and our thoughts and prayers are with his family," Carter stated.

Investigators from the FBI and Mexican law enforcement are collaborating with U.S. marshals to probe the circumstances of the death, Carter noted. An autopsy is scheduled to take place in Mexico, with the possibility of a second examination once Bustamante's remains are repatriated.
